verdict.reasoning: Patient states: “I have soreness in my fingers, and my finger, like, the skin on my hands is kind of cracked.”
Doctor asks: “Is it the skin on your hands mainly, that's dry?” Patient agrees and doctor later clarifies palm involvement: “Which part of your hands are affected? Mainly the palm.”
Doctor: “Have you noticed any itchiness in your palms?” Patient: “Yeah, it's itchy. Not all the time, but, yeah, it does get itchy.”
Timing and symptoms: Patient: “A couple of months ago. Like, three, four months ago.” plus initial complaint of “soreness… skin on my hands is kind of cracked.”
Palms: “Which part of your hands are affected? Mainly the palm.” Impact on work: “it's gotten to a point where it hurts a lot, and I can't really do my job… I do work as a housekeeper… it's a hotel.”
Bleeding with scratching: Doctor: “Scratching yourself often and bleeding?” Patient: “Yeah, I guess when I scratched it, yes, it has bled sometimes, but… otherwise it hasn't bled on its own.”
Leg dryness: Patient: “I have dryness, like, you know, in other parts, like my legs, but it's not… very… severe.” and later “it's just a little bit of dryness in my legs.”
Occupation and products: Patient: “I do work as a housekeeper… It's a hotel. I do the whole thing, like the bedroom, bathroom.” Also mentions using cleaning products (“bugs for bathrooms”).
Inconsistent glove use: “to be honest, I'm not always very good about wearing gloves” and “I usually use [gloves] for bathrooms, but… bedrooms and corridors. Not always.”
Job change timing: “I switched jobs four months ago.”

Doctor links exposure and symptoms: “I think you might have something called dermatitis or contact dermatitis… particularly people in your field who are using cleaning products, not using gloves. Sometimes get a bit of a reaction between the chemicals… and your skin.”

System review: Doctor asks about fever, nausea, vomiting, bowels, urine, appetite; patient answers no to systemic/abdominal/urinary symptoms and “Yeah, I feel good” to overall well-being and appetite.
Past medical history: Doctor: “do you have any other conditions at all?” Patient: “I have diabetes.”
Medications: Doctor: “Which medication do you take?” Patient: “Metformin.”
Combination of pmh-001 and med-001: patient has diabetes and takes metformin.
Doctor: “Do you have any allergies either to any medications or in general?” The transcript shows no allergy reported in response, implying no allergies documented.
Family history: Doctor: “Family history wise? Is there anything I should be aware of?” Patient: “Diabetes as well?” and confirms: “Yes.”
Smoking: Doctor: “Do you smoke at all?” Patient: “No.”
Alcohol: Doctor: “Do you drink much in the way of alcohol?” Patient: “Once a week. A couple of pints. A week?” Doctor: “A week. Okay, so very minimal alcohol there.”
Sporadic glove use: “I'm not always very good about wearing gloves” and “I usually use [gloves] for bathrooms, but… bedrooms and corridors. Not always.”
Transcript: “It's a hotel. I do the whole thing, like the bedroom, bathroom.” This is hotel (commercial) work only; there is no mention of residential settings.

Doctor: “I think you might have something called dermatitis or contact dermatitis… particularly people in your field who are using cleaning products, not using gloves… between the chemicals and your skin.” Chronicity and palmar involvement come from earlier statements (3–4 months, “Mainly the palm”).

Symptoms: patient reports “soreness… skin on my hands is kind of cracked,” “it's itchy,” and bleeding “when I scratched it… it has bled sometimes,” all used by doctor in forming dermatitis/contact dermatitis assessment.

Plan: “what we try and do is avoid the trigger. So in your case, I strongly recommend that you wear gloves when cleaning at all times.” The notion of avoiding triggers is explicit; reviewing products is implied by earlier discussion of products but not explicitly instructed; main glove/trigger advice is supported.

Doctor: “we can try some steroid creams to help with inflammation as well as some stronger emollients which you really need to kind of coat on throughout the day, three, four times a day for the next couple of weeks just to help with the moisturizing of your skin.”
Prescription: Patient asks where to get medicines; Doctor: “So I'll do a prescription for you now and send over to your pharmacy.” This follows discussion of steroid creams and emollients.
Doctor advises moisturizing and wearing gloves/avoiding triggers, but does not explicitly mention “monitor for signs of infection” or give specific education phrased as such.

Follow-up: “I think a minimum couple of weeks, 10 days to 14 days. And if it still hasn't got better, or indeed if it's getting worse, if it's spreading or dryness is getting worse, come back and see me sooner. … we can maybe think about other things we can give to you.”
